summary: Specifies extensions to Kerberos, called PKINIT, that integrate public key cryptography into the initial authentication exchange. Users can authenticate using asymmetric signature or encryption algorithms in the pre-authentication data fields rather than only a password-derived key. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: PKINIT adds public-key authentication to the initial Kerberos exchange between a client and a Key Distribution Center. After they establish the reply key, the client receives a ticket and continues with the ordinary Kerberos process.

subtitle: PKINIT uses public-key credentials for the initial Kerberos authentication exchange.

tldr.problem: In the normal Kerberos initial exchange, the reply key for a human user is typically derived from the user's password.
tldr.mechanism: The client signs a pre-authentication request with its private key and certificate. The KDC validates it and returns a signed reply using a key established by Diffie-Hellman or delivered with public-key encryption.
tldr.outcome: After the initial exchange, the client uses Kerberos tickets as usual. RFC 4556 has been updated by RFC 6112, RFC 8062 and RFC 8636.

today: RFC 4556 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 6112, RFC 8062 and RFC 8636. Read those updates with this specification.

sections.title: Why Add Public Keys to Kerberos
sections.content:
Kerberos V5 uses a Key Distribution Center (KDC) to issue tickets. In the initial Authentication Service exchange, the KDC encrypts its reply with an AS reply key, typically derived from a human user's password.

PKINIT adds asymmetric public-key cryptography to this initial exchange. The client and KDC use public and private key pairs to authenticate the exchange and establish the AS reply key. Later ticket requests continue to use Kerberos as specified in RFC 4120.
sections.plainLanguage: PKINIT lets the initial Kerberos exchange use public-key credentials instead of relying only on a password-derived key. Once the client receives its initial ticket, later Kerberos exchanges proceed as usual.

sections.title: The Client and KDC Exchange
sections.content:
The client includes a PKINIT pre-authentication element in its AS-REQ. It contains public-key information and a signature. The KDC checks the signature, the certificate path, the client's identity binding and its local authentication policy.

If the checks pass, the KDC returns an AS-REP with a second PKINIT pre-authentication element. It provides key information through Diffie-Hellman or public-key encryption. The client verifies the KDC's signature, obtains the reply key, decrypts the AS-REP and continues with Kerberos.
sections.plainLanguage: The client signs its initial request and sends certificate information. The KDC checks the request, then sends a signed reply that lets the client obtain the key for the Kerberos response.

sections.title: The Signed Client Request
sections.content:
The PA-PK-AS-REQ pre-authentication element contains a signed AuthPack. It includes a PKAuthenticator with a timestamp, a random nonce and a checksum of the KDC request body. The checksum must be present.

The AuthPack may also carry the client's Diffie-Hellman public value, supported CMS algorithms, a nonce used when Diffie-Hellman keys may be reused, and information about trusted certification authorities. The client's certificate chain helps the KDC build a path to a trust anchor; the request must not include root CA certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The client signs a package that includes a timestamp, a random value and a checksum of the request. It can also include a public value for Diffie-Hellman and its certificate chain.

sections.title: How the KDC Checks the Client
sections.content:
The KDC verifies the signature and validates the client's X.509 certificate. It checks that the public key is bound to the Kerberos principal named in the request, using its own binding or the certificate's Kerberos principal name. It also checks the request timestamp to detect replay.

Local policy can determine whether the KDC checks revocation status or requires an extended key usage for PKINIT client authentication. If the certificate, name binding, signature, timestamp or Diffie-Hellman parameters fail a required check, the KDC returns the corresponding Kerberos error.
sections.plainLanguage: The KDC checks that the signature is valid and that the certificate identifies the requested Kerberos principal. It also checks the timestamp and any local certificate or key-parameter rules.

sections.title: Two Ways to Deliver the Reply Key
sections.content:
Every implementation must support Diffie-Hellman key delivery. The KDC signs its public value and the client's nonce; both sides derive a shared secret and use it to produce the AS reply key. The RFC requires support for Oakley 1024-bit group 2 and 2048-bit group 14.

Public-key encryption is a recommended method. The KDC creates a reply key, signs it together with a checksum of the AS-REQ, and encrypts the key package to the client's public key. The client must verify the checksum in this method. The ticket lifetime must not exceed the validity period of the client's key pair.
sections.plainLanguage: With Diffie-Hellman, the client and KDC independently derive the same reply key. With public-key encryption, the KDC creates a key and encrypts it for the client.

sections.title: How the Client Checks the KDC
sections.content:
The client verifies the KDC's signature and certificate, including the binding between the signing key and the KDC for the target realm. If public-key encryption delivered the reply key, the client also verifies the AS-REQ checksum in the reply package.

Only after the applicable checks succeed does the client use the AS reply key to decrypt the response. The KDC can indicate support for PKINIT in a pre-authentication error by including an empty PA_PK_AS_REQ element.
sections.plainLanguage: The client verifies that the reply was signed by a KDC authorized for the target realm. It then uses the established reply key to decrypt the Kerberos response.

sections.title: Trust, Randomness and Denial of Service
sections.content:
PKINIT depends on strong random values, including Diffie-Hellman exponents. The client must also verify that the authority issuing a KDC certificate is authorized to issue certificates for the target realm; otherwise the certificate does not establish the KDC identity.

Kerberos error messages are not integrity protected, so an attacker can alter suggested Diffie-Hellman parameters. The RFC also notes that PKINIT has no return-routability test to prevent expensive public-key work triggered by requests. Reusing Diffie-Hellman keys can reduce processing per request, subject to the specified rules.
sections.plainLanguage: PKINIT depends on unpredictable secret values and correct certificate trust rules. The KDC also needs to consider the cost of public-key work triggered by requests.
